title: Claude writes formal proofs for 123 open-source libraries
friendlyTitle: Claude wrote mathematical proofs for 123 open-source libraries
summary: Anthropic and Theorem used Claude to prove that 239 test entry points across 123 OSS-Fuzz libraries will not crash on any input under 64 MB, under a narrow set of assumptions: a single-threaded RISC-V binary on a modeled Linux system. The proofs are about 180 million lines of Rocq. While writing them, Claude found and patched bugs that years of fuzzing had missed. Rocq checks the proofs. Anthropic is publishing a subset, and Theorem is offering the same pipeline to other open-source projects.
friendlySummary: Anthropic and a partner, Theorem, used Claude to prove that 239 test entry points in 123 open-source libraries will not crash on any input under 64 MB. The proof only holds for a narrow setup: one thread, a RISC-V processor, and a modeled Linux system. The proofs are about 180 million lines, checked by a proof tool called Rocq. While writing them, Claude found and patched bugs that years of random testing had missed. Anthropic is publishing some of the proofs. Theorem is offering the same pipeline to other open-source projects.
whyItMatters: A proof is not a guarantee that the software on your laptop is safe. It holds only for that processor, that single thread, and inputs under 64 MB. It does change the practical question: instead of hoping a fuzzer tried the bad input, you can check a machine-verified argument that no input in that range crashes the tested entry point.
friendlyWhyItMatters: This does not mean the copy of the software on your computer is safe. The proof covers one kind of chip, one thread, and inputs under 64 MB. What changes is the question you can ask. Instead of hoping a tester tried the bad input, you can check a machine-verified argument that no input in that range crashes the tested door into the code.
